title: Camus: a study of the four great works
author: Albert Camus
translator: a study written for this app (his books are still in copyright, so only short quotations are used)

body: ## The Stranger (1942)

Albert Camus finished The Stranger (in French L'Étranger, which also means "the outsider" and "the foreigner") in May 1940, in Paris, as the German army broke through into France. He was twenty-six, a journalist from Algiers, poor, tubercular, and almost unknown. The book was published in occupied Paris in 1942 and made him famous within a few years. It is short, about 120 pages, and it may be the most widely read French novel of the twentieth century.

Its first sentence is one of the most famous in literature. In French it is four words and a beat: "Aujourd'hui, maman est morte." Today, Maman died. Then, at once, the doubt: or maybe yesterday, I don't know. A telegram from the old people's home has said only that his mother has died, funeral tomorrow, deepest sympathy, and the narrator observes that this means nothing; perhaps it was yesterday.

Notice what has happened in two lines. A man tells you his mother is dead, and the first thing he shows you is not grief but uncertainty about a date, and a mild irritation with an imprecise telegram. You do not yet know whether to be shocked by him. That uncertainty is the whole book.
## Part One: the sun

The narrator is Meursault, a young clerk in a shipping office in Algiers, then a French city in North Africa. We never learn his first name. He asks his boss for two days off, and senses the boss is annoyed; he almost apologises, then thinks there is nothing to apologise for. He takes the bus to the home at Marengo, fifty miles away, in the heat.

At the vigil over his mother's coffin he does not ask to see her face. He accepts a café au lait from the caretaker, and then, because he likes to, he smokes. The old friends of his mother come in silently and sit opposite him, and one old woman weeps steadily, and he wishes she would stop. In the morning he follows the hearse through the blazing countryside, with an old man named Thomas Pérez, his mother's companion at the home, hobbling behind and cutting across the fields to keep up. Meursault notices the sweat, the tar melting on the road, the blood-red earth falling on the coffin. He feels the sun. He does not cry.

The next day, Saturday, he goes swimming in the harbour and meets Marie Cardona, a typist who used to work in his office. They swim, they go to a comic film with the actor Fernandel, she spends the night with him. On Sunday he stays in his flat and watches the street from his balcony all afternoon: families going for a walk, young men going to the cinema, the lamps coming on. He thinks: another Sunday over, Maman buried, I'm going back to work, and nothing has really changed.

Then Camus brings in the neighbours, and the book's quiet starts to darken. Old Salamano lives with a mangy spaniel he has had for eight years; he curses it and beats it twice a day, and they look alike, the narrator says, scabby and red. When the dog runs away, Salamano weeps through the wall at night. Raymond Sintès, a warehouse man everyone suspects of living off women, asks Meursault to write a letter for him: a woman, an Arab woman he says has cheated him, should be lured back so he can punish her. Meursault writes it. He has no reason not to. Later he hears Raymond beating her, and when the police come he agrees to testify that she cheated Raymond.

Marie asks him whether he loves her. He says it does not mean anything, but he probably doesn't. She asks if he will marry her. He says it makes no difference to him; if she wants to, they will. His boss offers him a promotion to an office in Paris, and he says it is all the same to him; one life is as good as another. The boss tells him he has no ambition.

Readers have called Meursault cold, empty, autistic, a monster, a saint. Camus himself said, in a preface he wrote for an American edition in 1955, that the hero is condemned because "he doesn't play the game". He will not say more than he feels. He will not say he loves Marie because he does not know that he does. He will not say he grieved because he did not grieve in the way people expected. He lies, Camus says, by omission sometimes, but never by saying more than is true.
## The beach

The killing comes at the end of Part One, and Camus writes it as if it were weather. Raymond invites Meursault and Marie to a beach cottage owned by a friend, Masson. Two Arab men have been following Raymond; one is the brother of the woman he beat. On the beach there is a fight; Raymond is cut with a knife. Later Raymond goes back with a revolver, and Meursault, to prevent a shooting, takes the gun from him.

Then Meursault walks back along the beach alone, in the white noon light, towards a spring behind a rock, because he wants the shade and the cool water. The brother is lying there. The heat is unbearable; the light on the sea is "a rain of fire"; the sweat runs into Meursault's eyes. He takes one step forward. The man draws his knife, and the light flashes off the blade into Meursault's forehead like a long sword. Everything wavers. His hand tightens on the revolver. He fires. And then, after a pause, he fires four more times into the body, and he says that it was like knocking four quick times on the door of unhappiness.
The Arab is never given a name in the novel. Hold on to that; we will come back to it.
## Part Two: the trial

In prison Meursault adapts, slowly. He misses women, then cigarettes, then learns to live without both; he finds that a man who had lived only one day could easily live a hundred years in prison, because he would have enough memories not to be bored. Under his mattress he finds an old scrap of newspaper telling a story, which he reads thousands of times: a man returns home rich after years abroad, takes a room at the inn his mother and sister run, without telling them who he is; that night they murder him for his money. Camus later turned it into a play, The Misunderstanding.

The examining magistrate waves a crucifix at him and asks whether he believes in God. Meursault says no. The magistrate is horrified: does he want his life to have no meaning? Asked whether he regrets what he did, Meursault says that rather than regret, he feels a kind of annoyance.

And then the trial, which is the most savage satire in the book. The court is hardly interested in the beach. It is interested in the funeral. The director of the home testifies that Meursault did not want to see his mother's body, did not cry, did not know her age. The caretaker says he smoked and drank coffee by the coffin. Marie is made to admit that the day after the funeral they went swimming and to a comic film and to bed. The prosecutor brings these facts together into a portrait of a man without a soul, and says he accuses this man of having buried his mother with a criminal heart.
When Meursault is finally asked why he killed the man, he says, too quickly and clumsily, that it was because of the sun. People in the courtroom laugh.

He is sentenced to have his head cut off in a public square in the name of the French people. Notice what has happened. He is being executed less for killing a man, which the court treats almost as a detail, than for not weeping at his mother's funeral. Camus put it bluntly in his 1955 preface: in our society, any man who doesn't cry at his mother's funeral runs the risk of being condemned to death.
## The last night

In the last chapter a prison chaplain insists on visiting him. Meursault refuses to see him three times. When the chaplain comes anyway and speaks of God, sin and the life to come, something breaks open in Meursault for the first time in the book. He grabs the priest by the collar and pours out everything: none of the priest's certainties is worth one hair of a woman's head; he, Meursault, has been right and is still right; nothing matters, since everyone is condemned; all are privileged, and all will die.

And then the anger empties him, and he is calm. He lies down, and smells the night, the earth and the salt, and hears the sounds of the countryside. For the first time, he says, he opens himself to "the gentle indifference of the world". Finding it so like himself, so brotherly, he feels that he has been happy, and that he is happy still. And his last wish, the last line, is that on the day of his execution there should be a large crowd, and that they should greet him with cries of hate.
## How to read it
There are three ways in, and the book holds all of them.

The first is the absurd. Meursault is a man who lives without the comforting stories: God, progress, a meaning given from outside. He lives by sensation (the sea, the sun, Marie's body, coffee, cigarettes) and he does not pretend. Society cannot bear this, because its rituals (grief at funerals, love declared, ambition, remorse) are partly ways of pretending that life has a meaning it may not have. Camus wrote The Myth of Sisyphus at the same time; the two books are a pair, one a story and one an argument.

The second is honesty. Camus, half-provocatively, called Meursault "the only Christ we deserve": a man who dies rather than lie. You do not have to like Meursault to feel the force of this. How often do you say more than you feel, because it is expected?

The third reading is the one the book did not see. The man Meursault kills is "the Arab". He has no name, no family we meet, no inner life. The court weighs Meursault's tears and barely mentions the dead man. This is colonial Algeria, where a French life and an Arab life were not weighed equally. In 2013 the Algerian writer Kamel Daoud published The Meursault Investigation, narrated by the dead man's brother, who gives him a name, Musa, and asks why the most famous murder in French literature has a victim no one remembers. It is now read alongside Camus's novel, and it is right that it should be.

Notice too how the book is written. The first part is in short, flat sentences, joined by "and" and "then", in the French past tense of conversation (the passé composé) rather than the literary past. Many critics heard in it the influence of Hemingway and of American hard-boiled crime fiction, which Camus admired. The style is the man: notation without commentary. Only on the beach, and on the last night, does the language catch fire.
## Before you go
Take three minutes and answer, in writing: is Meursault guilty of what he was condemned for? Then: is he guilty of what he did? The book is built on the gap between those two questions.
## The Myth of Sisyphus (1942): the argument in full

You may already have read the short essay on Sisyphus in this app. Here is the whole argument, step by step, because it is one of the clearest lines of thought in modern philosophy and it is short enough to carry in your head.

Camus wrote it between 1938 and 1941 and published it a few months after The Stranger. He called it an essay on the absurd, and he begins with a provocation: there is only one really serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide. To judge whether life is or is not worth living is to answer the fundamental question of philosophy; everything else (whether the world has three dimensions, whether the mind has nine or twelve categories) comes afterwards. He notes drily that he has never seen anyone die for the ontological argument.
## Step one: the feeling of the absurd

The absurd can strike anyone, anywhere, he says: at the corner of a street, in a restaurant's revolving door. And he gives the most famous description of how it arrives. You get up; you take the tram; four hours in the office or the factory; lunch; the tram again; four more hours; dinner; sleep; and Monday Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday and Saturday to the same rhythm. That road is easy to follow most of the time. But one day the "why" arises, and everything begins in that weariness tinged with amazement.

Other doors open onto the same feeling. Time: we live for tomorrow, for later, for when we are older, and one day we realise that tomorrow is carrying us towards death. Strangeness: a landscape, a stone, a familiar face suddenly looks foreign and closed. Other people: watch a man talking in a telephone box behind glass; you see his gestures but not his words, and wonder why he is alive. And death, which every argument walks around and none answers.
## Step two: what the absurd is, exactly

Camus is careful here. The world in itself is not absurd; it is simply there, unreasonable and silent. Human beings in themselves are not absurd; we have a deep longing for clarity, unity, a reason for things. The absurd is the confrontation between the two: our demand for meaning and the world's silence. It is a divorce, he says, and it exists only in the relation.
This gives him his rule. If the absurd is the only certainty we have, the honest thing is to keep it, not to escape from it. The question becomes: can one live with it, and how?
## Step three: the escapes he rejects

The first is physical suicide. To kill oneself is to admit that life is too much, that one has not understood it. But it does not solve the absurd; it abolishes one of its two terms, the human being who asks. Camus calls it a confession.

The second he calls philosophical suicide, and he spends some of the toughest pages of the book on it. He reviews the existentialist thinkers he admires, Kierkegaard, Jaspers, Chestov, and the phenomenologist Husserl, and finds that each of them, having seen the wall of the absurd, then leaps: into God, into the transcendent, into an all-embracing reason. They start from despair and end with hope. Camus treats this leap as an evasion. It is like stopping at the edge of the cliff and then deciding there must be a bridge.
## Step four: what he keeps
If you refuse both escapes, three consequences follow, and they are the core of the book.
Revolt: a constant confrontation with the absurd, a refusal to be reconciled, which gives life its value and its grandeur. Not hope, which looks away, but lucid defiance.

Freedom: if there is no eternal order and no tomorrow guaranteed, I am free of the false freedoms (ambitions, plans, the idea of a career as a destiny) that imprisoned me. A condemned man on the morning of his execution, Camus says, is indifferent to everything but the pure flame of life.
Passion: if no life has a meaning beyond itself, then what matters is not to live best but to live most: the quantity and intensity of experience, lived with full awareness.
## Step five: absurd lives

He then gives portraits of men who live like this, not as models but as illustrations. Don Juan, who loves each woman with the same passion and wholeness, without illusions of eternal love, and pays the price without complaint. The actor, who lives many lives in a single one, knowing each lasts the length of a performance. The conqueror, who acts in history knowing that history has no final meaning. And then the creator: the artist, the novelist, who creates without hope of explaining the world, who adds to it images of its own diversity. Art, for Camus, is the most absurd and most lucid of joys.
## Step six: Sisyphus

The book ends with the myth. Sisyphus had cheated the gods (in one version he chained up Death so that no one died), and in the underworld he is condemned to roll a rock to the top of a mountain, from which it rolls back down, for ever. Camus fixes on the moment when Sisyphus walks back down, after the rock: his hour of consciousness. He knows the whole extent of his wretched condition; it is what he thinks of during his descent. And the lucidity that should be his torture crowns his victory. There is no fate, Camus says, that cannot be surmounted by scorn.
His fate belongs to him. The rock is his thing. The struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. And then the six words that end the book: one must imagine Sisyphus happy.
## The Rebel (1951): from "I" to "we"

Nine years later Camus published a long, difficult, brave book, L'Homme révolté, The Rebel. The Myth of Sisyphus had asked whether one may kill oneself. The Rebel asks, after a war in which tens of millions were killed, often in the name of ideas: whether one may kill others.

It begins with a simple scene. A slave, who has taken orders all his life, suddenly says no. A limit has been crossed. But in saying no, he also says yes: yes, there is something in me that is worth more than your orders, a line you may not cross. And that something is not only his: the slave who rebels does it for all slaves. Camus put it in a formula that parodies Descartes: I rebel, therefore we exist.

From that root he traces two great histories. Metaphysical rebellion, against God and the human condition (from the Marquis de Sade through Ivan Karamazov to Nietzsche). And historical rebellion, the great revolutions (1789, 1917), which began from that no and ended, he argues, by justifying terror, the guillotine and the camps in the name of a perfect future. The rebel who forgets his limit becomes a new tyrant. Real rebellion, Camus says, has a measure built into it. It is the refusal to be a victim and also the refusal to be an executioner (the title of a series of articles he had written in 1946, Neither Victims nor Executioners).
## The quarrel

The Rebel destroyed one of the most famous friendships of the century. Jean-Paul Sartre, the leading philosopher in Paris, was then moving closer to the French Communist Party and defended the Soviet Union, whose labour camps Camus condemned. In 1952 Sartre's journal Les Temps modernes published a hostile review of The Rebel by Francis Jeanson. Camus replied angrily, addressing Sartre as "Monsieur le Directeur". Sartre answered publicly in a long, wounding letter that told Camus he had become a moralist without the right to judge, and that ended their friendship. They never reconciled. When Camus died, Sartre wrote a generous obituary. History, most would now say, proved Camus right about the camps.
## What to keep from today

From the Myth: the absurd is not the world but the meeting of your hunger for meaning with its silence; you need neither a leap nor despair; revolt, freedom and passion are enough. From The Rebel: every real no contains a yes, and every real rebellion has a limit. Write down the one you can use this week.
## The Plague (1947)

In 1947 Camus published his longest and most loved novel, La Peste, The Plague. It is set in Oran, a dull commercial city on the Algerian coast which, the narrator says, has no pigeons, no trees and no gardens. One April morning the rats start coming out to die in the streets and on the stairs, at first a few, then thousands. Then the people start dying. The authorities hesitate to name it; then they name it, and close the city gates. For almost a year no one may leave and no one may come in.

The book is told by a narrator who reveals his identity only at the end, and who writes like a chronicler: dry, careful, refusing to exaggerate. Around him is a small group of ordinary people who decide, without heroics, to fight the epidemic with what they have.

Jean Tarrou is a visitor stranded in the town, who keeps a notebook of odd details and who organises volunteer teams to fight the plague. Late one night he tells his story: his father was a prosecutor, and as a boy he watched him demand the death penalty for a frightened man in the dock. From that day Tarrou decided that he would never again be on the side of those who kill, even for good reasons; and he says the only question that interests him is how to become a saint without God.

Joseph Grand is a timid municipal clerk who spends his evenings rewriting the first sentence of a novel he will never finish (about a woman riding a horse through the Bois de Boulogne on a May morning), searching for the perfect adjective. Camus makes him, deliberately, the most unlikely hero of the book: he does the dull statistical work of the volunteer teams, every evening, without fuss.

Raymond Rambert is a journalist from Paris trapped in Oran, desperate to escape back to the woman he loves. For half the book he schemes with smugglers to get out. When the escape is finally arranged, he stays: he would be ashamed, he says, to be happy alone.

Father Paneloux is a Jesuit who preaches a fierce sermon early on, telling the town that the plague is God's punishment. Later he watches a child die in long agony, and he cannot say the same thing again. His second sermon is quieter and stranger: we must believe everything or deny everything, and he chooses to believe.
And there is Cottard, a petty criminal who is the only person in Oran who is happier during the plague, because while everyone is in danger, nobody is looking for him.
## Why it is about more than disease

Readers in 1947 understood at once that the plague was also the German occupation of France, which had just ended: the slow spread, the denial, the officials who wait, the people who collaborate and the few who resist, the exile of separation, the return of normal life that does not quite erase what happened. Camus had worked in the Resistance, editing the underground newspaper Combat. But the book is deliberately larger than any one event. The plague is whatever kills people while others look away. It returned to the bestseller lists across the world in 2020.

The novel's moral is not heroism. When Rambert talks about heroism, the narrator says that this whole business is not about heroism; it is about common decency, and the only way to fight the plague is decency, which means doing your job. Tarrou, in his notebook, says that each of us has the plague within us, and the good man is the one who is careful, who almost never infects anyone.

And the ending is not triumph. When the gates reopen and the city celebrates, the narrator remembers that the plague bacillus never dies or disappears for good; it can lie dormant for years in furniture and linen, in cellars and trunks and old papers, and perhaps the day will come when, for the bane and the enlightening of men, it will rouse up its rats again and send them forth to die in a happy city.
## The Fall (1956)

Camus's last finished novel is short, dark and strange, and many critics think it is his finest. It is a single monologue, spoken over five days by a Frenchman in a seedy sailors' bar in Amsterdam called the Mexico City. He speaks to a stranger, a fellow Frenchman who happens to be at the bar, and we hear only his side. His name, he says, is Jean-Baptiste Clamence: John the Baptist, the voice crying (clamans) in the wilderness.

He was once a celebrated Paris lawyer who defended widows and orphans, helped the blind across the street, gave up his seat on the bus, and was admired by everyone, above all by himself. He lived, he says, on the heights. Then two things happened.

One evening, crossing the Pont des Arts in Paris, satisfied with himself, he heard behind him a laugh, a good, quiet laugh, that seemed to come from nowhere. Nobody was there. From that night he could not stop hearing it, and began to see his own virtue as a performance.

And then he tells the secret he has been circling for days. Two or three years before the laugh, one November night after midnight, he crossed the Pont Royal and passed a slim young woman in black leaning over the parapet. He had gone fifty yards when he heard the sound of a body hitting the water, then a cry, several times, going downstream. He stood still. He told himself it was too late, too far, and he walked away. He did not read the newspapers for days.

Since then he has made himself what he calls a judge-penitent. He confesses his faults to strangers in bars, at length and brilliantly, until his listener recognises himself in the portrait; and then, having confessed, Clamence feels entitled to judge. Every man, he says, testifies to the crime of all the others. It is a sermon and a trap; you feel its pull as you read.

The book ends with Clamence, feverish, imagining the young woman throwing herself into the water again, so that he might, a second time, have the chance of saving them both. Then he takes it back: it is too late now, it will always be too late. And he adds one last word: fortunately.
## The invincible summer

Camus also wrote lyrical essays, and the most quoted line he ever wrote comes from one of them, Return to Tipasa (1952), about the Roman ruins on the Algerian coast where he had been happy as a young man. Returning in winter, in a dark time of his life, he writes that in the midst of winter he found that there was in him an invincible summer. People who have never read a page of Camus have this sentence on their walls.
## The Nobel Prize and the end

In 1957, at forty-four, Camus received the Nobel Prize in Literature, one of the youngest laureates ever. The war in Algeria was at its height, and he was attacked from all sides for refusing to support either the French army or the terror of the independence movement. At a meeting with students in Stockholm, an Algerian student challenged him; Camus answered that people were planting bombs in the tramways of Algiers, that his mother might be on one of those trams, and that if that was justice, he preferred his mother. The sentence was shortened in the press into a slogan, and argued about for decades.

He wrote to his old schoolteacher, Louis Germain, the day after the announcement: without him, without the affectionate hand he held out to the poor child that he was, none of this would have happened.

On 4 January 1960 Camus died in a car crash near Villeblevin, south of Paris. He was forty-six. In his bag was the manuscript of an autobiographical novel about his childhood in Algiers, The First Man; it was published in 1994.
## Camus in one page

The world does not answer our demand for meaning (the absurd). We do not need to escape that fact by despair or by a leap of faith. We can live it in revolt, freedom and passion (Sisyphus). Every real rebellion says yes to a shared human dignity and has a limit: neither victims nor executioners (The Rebel). In the face of evil, what is asked is not heroism but decency, doing your job, refusing to look away (The Plague). Beware the man who confesses only to earn the right to judge (The Fall). And keep, through every winter, the summer you know is in you.
## Read next, when you can

The Stranger and The Fall are short enough for an evening each, and they are worth owning on paper. Read them in a modern translation (Matthew Ward's Stranger, 1988, or Sandra Smith's, 2012). Then The Plague, then, when you are ready, the essays.
